outcome: Chen–Chen–Chen (arXiv:2411.16146, Nov 2024) proved that every divisorial contraction to a curve between terminal threefolds is a weighted blow-up under a suitable embedding, and as Theorem 1.3 deduced that there exists a surface S containing the contracted curve C with at worst Du Val singularities — i.e. a general elephant with Du Val singularities — extending the previously known irreducible-fiber case (Kollár–Mori) to this broader class of contractions. Separately, Prokhorov's paper on general elephants for extremal curve germs with reducible central curve (arXiv:2002.10693) was revised to v5 in September 2024, adding an appendix, and Mori–Prokhorov (arXiv:2410.03165, Oct 2024, v2 Apr 2025) gave a rough classification of extremal curve germs with reducible central curve that the authors note has direct consequences for the general elephant conjecture via their earlier Theorem 1.3 in a companion paper. None of this resolves the conjecture in general — flipping contractions, contractions to points, and further conic-bundle/reducible-curve configurations remain open — but each is a genuine case of the stated problem being settled, so the overall status is `partial`.
summary: The frozen Wikipedia bullet asks whether 'general elephants have at most Du Val singularities' for threefolds — this is M. Reid's general elephant conjecture, a long-running program (Reid 1987 origin; Kawakita 2003 for divisorial contractions to points; Kollár–Mori for irreducible-fiber extremal curve germs; Prokhorov 1996+ for Mori conic bundles) that has been settled case by case over three decades, with genuine counterexamples known in the non-Gorenstein Q-Fano setting (Iano-Fletcher) predating the window. Since 26 Jan 2024, three pieces of progress fall in the window: (1) arXiv:2411.16146 (Chen–Chen–Chen, submitted 25 Nov 2024, v1 only) proves that divisorial contractions to curves between terminal threefolds are weighted blow-ups, and its Theorem 1.3 explicitly proves the general elephant conjecture for this class (confirmed directly by fetching the paper's HTML and reading the theorem statement, which contradicts an earlier automated summary that claimed no elephant/Du-Val mention — the terms are present and central to Theorem 1.3). (2) arXiv:2002.10693 (Mori–Prokhorov-adjacent; solo Prokhorov-line paper on extremal curve germs with reducible central curve) was revised to v5 on 23 Sept 2024, adding Appendix B and correcting one introductory sentence — a within-window event but a minor revision of a paper whose substantive case (condition (*) on the curve components) was already established in earlier versions predating the window, so I did not treat the v5 date as establishing new mathematical content, only used 2411.16146 as the load-bearing event. (3) arXiv:2410.03165 (Mori–Prokhorov, Oct 2024, v2 Apr 2025) gives a rough classification of extremal curve germs with reducible central curve, which the authors note has consequences for the general elephant conjecture via a companion theorem, but I could not confirm this paper itself states a Du Val/elephant conclusion directly (fetched content showed no 'elephant' occurrence), so I treat it as related but did not use it as the primary event. All three lines of work are classical algebraic geometry (minimal model program, extremal contractions, weighted blow-ups); no source mentions AI, machine learning, or any computer-assisted proof tool. This is a case of the problem, not the whole problem: the conjecture remains open for other classes of extremal contractions (flips, more general reducible-curve and conic-bundle configurations), so status is `partial` rather than `resolved`, with `resolution_direction` `confirmed` since the settled case went the conjectured way (Du Val singularities do occur, no counterexample in this class).
competing_reading: One could argue this is really an `open` record because the *general* conjecture (as loosely worded by Wikipedia, with no restriction to a class of contractions) is unresolved and always has been, and the incremental case-by-case literature has existed since the 1990s — so nothing distinctively new happened 'to the problem' in the sense a casual reader of the Wikipedia bullet would mean. Under §3.1's rule, however, a settled case of the stated question counts as `partial`, and Theorem 1.3 of 2411.16146 is squarely a case (divisorial contractions to curves) of the stated question (do general elephants have Du Val singularities), so I classify it as `partial` rather than `open`.
what_would_settle_it: A full resolution would require settling the conjecture for the remaining classes of extremal contractions (flipping contractions and the remaining reducible-central-curve / conic-bundle cases), or a counterexample within the terminal threefolds setting (as opposed to the known non-Gorenstein Q-Fano counterexamples, which are for a different, related global existence-of-elephant question rather than the local Du Val question).
